reasons: No test is visible in this file.
Rates are yearly averages and nearest-year proxies, so results are approximate by design.

terms.meaning: how many units of a local currency equal one US dollar
the average exchange rate across one whole year
a rate from a nearby year used because the exact year is not published
a published data set of exchange rates kept by the World Bank
how much the actual budget exceeds the planned budget, as a percentage

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose and rate source
sections.what: Explains that the rates come from a generated table of yearly averages, and that every converted value carries its rate year and reason.
sections.why: The rate table is generated by a script, so the file only reads from it.
sections.watch_out: The table must be regenerated to add new years or currencies, and this file does not do that.

sections.name: WB_ECONOMY, FxPoint
sections.title: Currency to economy mapping
sections.what: Maps each currency code to the World Bank economy whose rate series holds it, for many currencies.
sections.why: The World Bank series is labelled by country rather than currency, so the mapping links the two.
sections.watch_out: A currency missing from this mapping cannot be sourced from the World Bank series.

sections.name: fxRate
sections.title: Finding an exchange rate for a year
sections.what: Returns the annual rate for a currency and year. For US dollars it returns one. If the year is missing, it uses the latest year held. If the exact year is not held, it uses the nearest held year, with the later year winning a tie.
sections.why: Gives a usable rate even when the exact year is not published, and records that it is a proxy.
sections.watch_out: Currencies with no series return only a reason, so the caller must check for that before using the rate.

sections.name: UsdConversion
sections.title: Shape of a conversion result
sections.what: Defines the converted record: currency, original amount, US dollar amount, rate, year used, the year asked for, the basis for that year, whether it is a proxy, the source and a note.
sections.why: Keeps the full reasoning with the number so no one has to guess how it was calculated.
sections.watch_out: Fields such as the requested year can be empty, so code reading them must allow for that.

sections.name: toUsdMillions
sections.title: Converting to US dollars
sections.what: Converts an amount in millions into US dollar millions at the rate for the chosen year, rounded to two decimals. It writes a note that shows the division, the year used and whether a proxy was needed. A US dollar input gets a note saying no conversion was done.
sections.why: The note lets a reader verify the number without the code.
sections.watch_out: The rounding is to two decimals of millions, so very small amounts can lose precision.

sections.name: yearOf
sections.title: Reading a year from a date
sections.what: Takes a date object or text such as a full date or just a year, and returns the year as a number, or nothing if no year is found.
sections.why: Dates arrive in several forms, and the conversion needs only the year.
sections.watch_out: Text is matched on the first four digits starting with 19 or 20, so text that starts with another number will return nothing.

sections.name: yardCostDeviation
sections.title: Cost overrun percentage
sections.what: Works out the percentage by which actual cost exceeds plan. If both figures were reported in the same non-US currency, it uses those amounts so that exchange rate changes do not look like overruns. Otherwise it compares US dollar figures. It returns nothing when a figure is missing or the plan is zero or less.
sections.why: Stops a currency swing between two years from being reported as a cost overrun.
sections.watch_out: The matching check allows a very small tolerance, so an unusual rounding could make the reported-currency route fall back to the dollar route.

summary: Converts money amounts from local currencies into US dollars using yearly average exchange rates, and works out cost overruns in a consistent currency.
purpose: Lets the app compare projects in different countries using one currency, and keeps a clear record of which rate year was used.
why: The header states that every conversion must show its rate year and reason, so a reader can check exactly what was done.
how: It looks up the annual rate for a currency and year, or the nearest held year if the exact year is missing. It then divides the amount by that rate and writes a plain note explaining the calculation. For cost overruns it compares planned and actual budgets in the same non-US currency when both are available, and otherwise compares US dollar figures.
inputs: An amount in millions, a currency code, a year or date, and a short text saying where the year came from. For overruns, the planned and actual US dollar figures and any conversion records.
outputs: A conversion record with the US dollar amount, the rate used, the year used, whether it was a proxy and an explanatory note. For overruns, a percentage, the basis used and the currency.
risks: A missing or unsupported currency returns only a reason, so callers must check for it. Using the nearest year means the rate may not match the true year. The overrun percentage returns nothing when the planned figure is zero or negative.
debug: If a figure looks wrong, read the note text in the conversion record: it shows the rate, the year and any proxy. If a currency gives no result, check whether it is in the rate table and in the economy mapping.
